rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
$$\text{Glass-transition temperature }T_{g}:\ \text{softening region of an amorphous solid}$$
$$\text{Bragg's law (X-ray identification of crystals): }n\lambda=2d\sin\theta$$

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: ❌ Amorphous solids are true solids with a very high viscosity. ✅ They are regarded as pseudo-solids or supercooled liquids because they lack long-range order and flow over long times.  ·  ❌ All solids have sharp melting points. ✅ Amorphous solids soften over a range (glass-transition temperature); only crystalline solids melt sharply.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Quartz, diamond and graphite are allotropic forms of giant covalent crystals; graphite is anisotropic (conducts along layers).  ·  Glass is a supercooled liquid — very old window glass is measurably thicker at the bottom because of slow flow.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: **Problem:** Why does glass not show a sharp melting point on heating? **Solution:** amorphous solids lack a periodic lattice, so bonds break over a range of energies — the material softens gradually between the glass-transition and melting regions instead of melting at one temperature.  ·  **Problem:** Graphite conducts electricity while diamond does not, though both are carbon. **Solution:** in graphite each carbon uses three of four valence electrons in σ bonds; the fourth electron is delocalised between layers enabling conduction, whereas in diamond all four electrons are localised in σ bonds.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Covers only: solid state, types of solids, amorphous, crystalline solids (within States of Matter).  ·  Out of scope here: topics of neighbouring units in Chemistry — don't mix them.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ### 1. Meaning of the solid state  ·  A solid has a definite shape and volume because its constituent particles are held in fixed mean positions by strong intermolecular (or interatomic/ionic) forces. The particles can only vibrate about their positions, so solids are rigid, practically incompressible and diffuse extremely slowly.…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Amorphous silicon is used in thin-film solar cells and LCD backplanes, where its cheaper deposition outweighs its lower efficiency.  ·  answer pattern for "Solid state: types of solids, amorphous and crystalline s…": define → method → result. Structure earns the marks on 6–10 mark questions.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: ### 2. Crystalline solids  ·  The particles are arranged in a regular, repeating three-dimensional pattern called a **crystal lattice**, which extends over a long range (long-range order). Properties: definite geometrical shape (crystal habit), sharp melting point, cleavage along definite planes, anisotropic physical properties (refractive index, thermal expansion, conductivity differ along different…  ·  ### 3. Types of crystalline solids (by binding force)

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ Isotropy means the same as anisotropy. ✅ Isotropic = same property in all directions (amorphous); anisotropic = direction-dependent (single crystals).  ·  ❌ Graphite is a molecular solid. ✅ Graphite is a covalent network with strong covalent layers held by weak van der Waals forces — which explains its lubricity and conductivity.  ·  ❌ Metals melt at high temperature because they are covalently bonded. ✅ Metallic bonding strength varies widely; Hg melts at −39 °C while W melts at 3422 °C.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Mention that amorphous solids are metastable and that polycrystalline materials lie between the two extremes.  ·  Distinguish between crystalline and amorphous solids on any six points.  ·  Classify crystalline solids according to the nature of the binding force and give two examples of each type.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Explain why diamond is extremely hard and why glass softens over a range of temperature.  ·  Compare the melting behaviour and X-ray diffraction patterns of crystalline and amorphous solids.  ·  State the limitations of the crystalline/amorphous classification.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: • **Ionic:** ions held by strong electrostatic forces (NaCl, CaF₂) — hard, brittle, high melting point, non-conducting as solids but conducting when molten or in solution, soluble in polar solvents.  ·  • **Covalent (network/atomic):** atoms joined by a continuous network of covalent bonds (diamond, graphite, SiC, quartz) — extremely hard, very high melting point, usually insulators or semiconductors (graphite conducts).  ·  • **Molecular:** molecules held by weak van der Waals forces or hydrogen bonds (iodine, dry ice, naphthalene, sugar, ice) — soft, low melting point, volatile, poor conductors.
